Lesson 1

Idea generation: eight formulas for instant answers

Stop hunting for the perfect idea. Pick the formula that matches your mental roadblock, say its trigger thought, and fill in the structure.

Traditional brainstorming is a trap

It produces slow, irrelevant and undefendable ideas.

The problem

  • Doubt
  • Overthink
  • Random
  • Slow
  • Panic
  • Vague
  • Chaos
  • Forget
  • No plan
  • Mess
The brainstorming flaw

Attempting to think of every possible idea results in a flood of irrelevant concepts you cannot confidently explain in English. It wastes critical minutes.

The solution

  1. 1Match a formula to your roadblock
  2. 2Say its trigger thought
  3. 3Fill in the structure
The reality check

Stop trying to invent the perfect, most profound idea. The examiner is not grading your IQ; they are grading your English execution. You need a framework to grab the closest workable idea instantly.

Every Band 9 idea shares three traits

The Band 9 idea

Relevant

It answers the specific prompt directly. Straying into a tangent guarantees a Band 5 for Task Achievement.

Developable

You possess the specific vocabulary and real-world examples required to expand upon it for a full paragraph.

Quick

The idea surfaces in seconds, not minutes. If it requires deep philosophical pondering, abandon it.

The eight formulas, with sample answers

Each formula has a trigger thought, a structure, the answer from the lesson slide, and ten more sample answers on different topics. Turn labels off to read an answer as continuous speech.

Examiners grade your language, not how brilliant your ideas are

The golden rule

Stop stressing over finding the perfect idea. Perfection causes hesitation. Use these frameworks to lock onto the closest workable idea instantly, and put your mental energy into executing it flawlessly with excellent grammar and vocabulary.

Lesson 2 (IELTS Speaking Part 1)

From long to developed

A longer answer isn’t a better answer. This lesson shows why some Part 1 responses feel flat even when the grammar is fine, gives you one formula to fix it, then a drill to practise on.

Long is not the same as developed

Many long Part 1 answers are grammatically fine. They’re weak because they don’t develop one idea; they just list several. A short, well-developed answer will almost always sound stronger.

What a weak answer does Idea→Idea→Idea→Idea→repetition
What a strong answer does Point→Why→Explanation→Example→Result
Don’t try to speak for longer. Try to make one idea clearer.

Five steps, one idea

Every strong answer follows roughly the same shape. It isn’t a script to memorise word for word; it’s a sequence to think through while you’re speaking.

    Same question, two answers

    Notice the weak version lists things. The strong one follows the formula above and leans on one or two natural phrases instead of ten.

    The quick test: can I ask “why?”

    After any answer, ask whether a listener could naturally reply “why is that important to you?” If yes, the idea needs more development. The why should already be inside the answer.

    Borrow the language, don’t recite it

    Pick one or two of these per topic, not all of them. Sprinkling the same idiom into every answer is what makes speech sound memorised rather than natural. Select a highlighted phrase in the passage to jump to its explanation, or open any phrase in the list.

    Phrases and collocations

    Practice drill

    Answer out loud first, then reveal the two model versions. Read the weak one and ask “what’s missing?” before you look at the strong one.

    All done

    Shuffle to go again, or restart to review in the original order.
